endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: A GenAIenabled device that has been benchmarked against a defined set of capabilities for premarket authorization could potentially be “re-benchmarked” against the same capabilities following a modification, providing evidence to determine whether the modification has affected safety or effectiveness of the device.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether re-benchmarking generative AI devices against their premarket capability baseline after modifications detects capability regression or prevents harm. The recommendation currently rests on a single regulatory discussion paper that presents re-benchmarking as a possible approach.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is a discussion paper that uses conditional language ("could potentially be"), which signals a proposal rather than a finding.

The endorsing discussion paper suggests that a premarket capability benchmark could be reused after a modification to judge whether safety or effectiveness changed. This framing resembles existing change-control thinking for devices, but the paper does not specify benchmark content, cadence, or thresholds. The paper treats the idea as a consideration rather than a requirement.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare generative AI device performance before and after updates on fixed capability benchmarks, measure how often re-benchmarking detects regressions that routine monitoring misses, and estimate the effort required at different update cadences and impact levels.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A benchmark built without these groups may not detect regressions that affect them, such as degraded performance in non-English or plain-language outputs.
